interrogated_candidate_name: Conserved Interaction Budget: Discretionary Ties Decay as Effort Reallocates to Role-Anchored Ties

exchanges.question: The mechanism's load-bearing premise is that 'the role boundary is the line between mandated and discretionary ties' — within-unit workflow ties are posited as role-mandated (and so survive co-location loss), cross-unit ties as discretionary/ambient-prompted (and so collapse). What observation would actually refute this? Concretely: if a cross-unit tie that is unambiguously role-mandated by the work flow (e.g. a cross-functional product/engineering-design interface required to ship) either collapsed or held after the shift, and a within-unit tie that was clearly ambient-dependent collapsed, could the theory distinguish 'the mechanism predicted this' from 'I relabeled the tie to fit'?
exchanges.assessment: The theory does make a directional, in-principle falsifiable prediction (asymmetry: cross-unit change < within-unit change, with totals conserved). But the mapping between the two theoretically distinct constructs — 'boundary-crossing' and 'discretionary' — is asserted by construction and hedged only with the word 'principally' ('principally within-unit workflow ties... principally cross-unit ties'). That hedge is precisely an explain-away route: a cross-unit tie that survived can be re-described as 'principally role-mandated', and a within-unit tie that decayed can be re-described as 'ambient-dependent'. The candidate offers no independent measurement that pins a tie's mandated-vs-discretionary status prior to observing its fate, and no defense that workflow mandates actually run along the functional boundary in the focal firm. Worse, the anchor literatures show this premise is not generally true: Van Den Bulte & Moenaert (1998) found R&D-to-marketing communication frequency was NOT affected by physical distance because 'business procedures accompanying the relocation prevented a widening gap' — i.e., cross-boundary ties can be mandate/procedure-anchored rather than ambient-prompted. So the core mechanism is falsifiable only for the clean cases and is protected by relabeling for exactly the ambiguous cases that matter most. Thin, not fatal: the directional prediction still constrains outcomes. Verdict: weak.

exchanges.question: The relation_form is explicitly a 'Reallocation under a conserved total (zero-sum reshuffle)': total maintenance effort is constant while it shifts toward within-unit ties. If the budget is conserved and the cross-unit subset loses effort, that freed effort must reappear as an INCREASE in within-unit interaction. But the phenomenon card records within-group contacts as 'stayed the same or increased.' If the data showed within-unit interaction exactly flat while cross-unit ties collapsed, would the theory be refuted (the freed effort evaporated, so there was no reshuffle) or would it still be 'explained'? And is 'total maintenance effort is conserved' an independent prediction or simply a restatement of the observed unchanged logged hours and meeting time?
exchanges.assessment: This is the mechanism's zero-sum backbone, and it is under-tested. Of the theory's three observable implications, two — (a) totals unchanged and (b) cross-unit collapse — are read directly off the phenomenon card rather than generated independently, and the third — (c) within-unit rise sufficient to absorb the freed effort — is only half-supported ('stayed the same or increased'). If within-unit were flat, the 'conserved reshuffle' would be contradicted (effort would have vanished, not reallocated), yet the candidate's phrasing gives no criterion for when 'stayed the same' falsifies the conservation claim versus when it is compatible. The result is a real risk that 'conservation' is inferred from the very observation it is meant to explain (curve-fitting / unfalsifiable-by-construction). It is not infinitely elastic — a flat-within-unit or expanding-total observation would count as a refuter — but the theory does not commit to that reading, so its central 'conserved budget' claim is weakly testable. Verdict: weak.

exchanges.question: The stated boundary conditions are 'functional units are the containers of formal roles' and 'total working hours and meeting time are administratively fixed, so the maintenance budget cannot expand.' Does the mechanism actually hold in a different setting — specifically (i) where cross-unit ties ARE role-mandated (matrix organizations, cross-functional product teams, liaison/coordinator roles) so that the role boundary does not coincide with the functional boundary, and (ii) where the interaction budget is NOT administratively fixed (salaried knowledge workers who can work longer, or cultures where remote work increases logged hours)? And does the assumption field honestly state the premise it depends on, or dodge the conditions under which the mechanism breaks?
exchanges.assessment: The assumption field is comparatively candid: it names 'tie maintenance is effort-limited', 'allocate preferentially to role-embedded ties', and 'cross-boundary maintenance depended on an ambient prompt rather than on the tie's recognized value'. That is honest. But the boundary condition is asserted, not defended, and it is plausibly violated by the very setting under study: large technology companies routinely organize cross-functional product work (engineering/product/design) as role-mandated, so 'functional unit = container of formal roles' may fail in the focal firm, which would make the ambient-prompt account wrong for a subset of the collapsed ties. The candidate would need to show, not assume, that the functional boundary is also the mandate boundary. On the second condition (fixed budget), the card itself says totals were 'almost the same' / 'roughly unchanged' — weaker than 'administratively fixed' — and in expandable-budget settings the conserved-total premise degrades from a mechanism to an empirical coincidence. Related evidence: Van Den Bulte & Moenaert (1998) show cross-boundary communication can be immune to distance when procedures mandate it; Suh et al. (2011) show the within/across-group composition effects of virtuality depend on group-level dispersion and technology support — i.e. the outcome is context-contingent, not a fixed rule. Verdict: weak.

exchanges.question: Is 'conserved interaction budget' plus a 'boundary-selective composition shift' actually a new construct, or an existing one wearing a new name? In particular, is the Y — the allocation of work-related contact across boundary-crossing vs boundary-contained ties as a function of co-location/virtuality — already an established dependent variable, and is the observed pattern (within-group ties hold/rise while cross-group ties collapse) already documented, such that the candidate's claim that 'existing constructs cannot generate a pattern in which total logged hours and meeting time are unchanged while only the boundary-crossing subset collapses' overreaches?
exchanges.assessment: I searched independently rather than trusting the candidate's self-report that it merely 'modifies Kleinbaum (2018)'. Two findings cut against the novelty claim for the Y and the phenomenon: (1) Suh, Shin, Ahuja & Kim (2011, JMIS) explicitly model 'intra-group tie strength and extra-group network range' as the dependent variable of virtuality — the composition outcome is already an established construct; (2) Zuzul et al. (2025, Management Science), analyzing 360B+ emails across 4,361 organizations through the COVID co-location shock, document exactly the boundary-selective pattern the candidate claims anchor theory 'cannot generate': organizations 'became more siloed... evidenced by increased modularity' and employees 'limited their communication to other members of that community'. That is the phenomenon, in the anchor journal, uncited. So the claim that existing constructs cannot generate a composition-only shift is contradicted empirically. On the other hand, the narrow mechanism — an effort-limited conserved budget with triage between ambient-prompted and role-mandated ties — was not found as an existing UTD24 construct: targeted searches for 'communication budget'/'interaction budget'/'communication capacity', 'tie maintenance' + cost/effort/capacity, 'communication' + 'zero-sum', and 'network' + 'reallocation' returned no equivalent formulation (the 'reallocation' hits were all operations/finance, not tie-maintenance). So this is a genuine within-tradition reframing of Kleinbaum (2018) with a new mechanism layer, not a pure relabel — but its Y and its empirical pattern are pre-existing and uncited. Verdict: weak.

cited_evidence.title: Dynamic Silos: Increased Modularity and Decreased Stability in Intraorganizational Communication Networks During the COVID-19 Pandemic
cited_evidence.relevant_snippet: We found that in 2020, organizations around the world became more siloed than in 2019, evidenced by increased modularity. This shift was concurrent with decreased stability within silos. ... At the same time, once in a subcommunity, they limited their communication to other members of that community. We term these network changes dynamic silos.
cited_evidence.abstract: Workplace communications around the world were drastically altered by the COVID-19 pandemic, related work-from-home orders, and the rise of remote work. To understand these shifts, we analyzed aggregated, anonymized metadata from over 360 billion emails within 4,361 organizations worldwide. By comparing month-to-month and year-over-year metrics, we examined changes in network community structures over the 24 months before and after COVID-19. We also examined shifts across multiple communication media (email, instant message, video call, and calendaring software) within a single global organization and compared them with communications shifts that were driven by changes in formal organizational structure. We found that in 2020, organizations around the world became more siloed than in 2019, evidenced by increased modularity. This shift was concurrent with decreased stability within silos. Collectively, our analyses indicate that following the onset of COVID-19, employees' communications began to shift more dynamically between subcommunities (teams, workgroups, or functional areas). At the same time, once in a subcommunity, they limited their communication to other members of that community. We term these network changes dynamic silos. We provide initial insights into the meaning and implications of dynamic silos for the future of work. This paper was accepted by Lamar Pierce, organizations.

cited_evidence.title: The influence of virtuality on social networks within and across work groups: A multilevel approach
cited_evidence.relevant_snippet: we develop a multilevel research framework that explores the effects of different levels of virtuality on one's intra-group tie strength and extra-group network range ... the individual-level virtuality (use of personal and communal communication technologies) significantly influences one's intra-group tie strength and extra-group network range. Moreover, the results show that the effects of individual-level virtuality on social networks vary depending on the group-level virtuality, such as geographic/temporal dispersion and technological support.
cited_evidence.abstract: We examine how the virtuality of work context influences individuals' social networks within and across work groups. Given this purpose, we develop a multilevel research framework that explores the effects of different levels of virtuality on one's intra-group tie strength and extra-group network range based on the computer-mediated communication theory, the proximity theory, and the social network theory. The results of the hierarchical linear modeling indicate that the individual-level virtuality (use of personal and communal communication technologies) significantly influences one's intra-group tie strength and extra-group network range. Moreover, the results show that the effects of individual-level virtuality on social networks vary depending on the group-level virtuality, such as geographic/temporal dispersion and technological support. By illuminating how individuals' social networks can be developed through the appropriate use of personal and communal communication technologies in the context of a virtual group, this study provides useful insights into the mechanics that underlie effective virtual work.

cited_evidence.title: Reorganization and tie decay choices
cited_evidence.relevant_snippet: Whereas most research on network evolution has focused on the role of interaction opportunities in the formation of new ties, this paper addresses tie decay choices. When the opportunity structure gets reorganized, social actors make choices about which ties to retain and which to allow to decay, informed by their past experience of the tie. ... people ... choose to retain ties to valuable contacts, they retain reciprocated ties ... and they retain socially embedded ties.
cited_evidence.abstract: Whereas most research on network evolution has focused on the role of interaction opportunities in the formation of new ties, this paper addresses tie decay choices. When the opportunity structure gets reorganized, social actors make choices about which ties to retain and which to allow to decay, informed by their past experience of the tie. I argue that, conditional on changes in opportunity, people (especially those with Machiavellian personalities) choose to retain ties to valuable contacts, they retain reciprocated ties (especially with highly empathic others), and they retain socially embedded ties (especially if they are low self-monitors). The empirical design, which exploits a randomized natural experiment, confirms these hypotheses and suggests that our understanding of tie decay choices—and, consequently, of network evolution—is enhanced by an integrated theoretical perspective that encompasses both social structure and social psychology. This paper was accepted by Olav Sorenson, organizations.

cited_evidence.title: The effects of R&D team co-location on communication patterns among R&D, marketing, and manufacturing
cited_evidence.relevant_snippet: Our results show that communication among R&D teams was enhanced after co-locating these teams. Surprisingly, communication frequency between R&D and marketing was not affected by the increased physical distance. This may suggest that business procedures accompanying the relocation prevented a widening gap between R&D and marketing. Alternatively, it may indicate that the effect of co-location depends on the content and medium of the communication flows.
cited_evidence.abstract: Reducing the physical distance among R&D engineers and between R&D and marketing is widely believed to result in more frequent communication, and hence higher product development performance. However, the empirical evidence for the effect of co-location on communication frequency is problematic for two reasons: (1) the evidence often features either little contextual realism or doubtful internal validity, and (2) the analysis does not deal with the statistical problems typical of network data. Our study avoids the first problem by using sequential network data collected from a quasi-experiment at an industrial company that regrouped its R&D teams into a new facility. We avoid the second problem by using Wasserman and Iacobucci's (1988) method for the statistical analysis of sequential network data. Our results show that communication among R&D teams was enhanced after co-locating these teams. Surprisingly, communication frequency between R&D and marketing was not affected by the increased physical distance. This may suggest that business procedures accompanying the relocation prevented a widening gap between R&D and marketing. Alternatively, it may indicate that the effect of co-location depends on the content and medium of the communication flows.

unanswered_weaknesses: The load-bearing identity 'role boundary = boundary between mandated and discretionary ties' is asserted rather than defended, and is plausibly false in the focal setting: large tech firms typically organize cross-functional product work (engineering/product/design) as role-mandated. If so, a subset of the collapsed cross-unit ties were mandate-anchored, and the ambient-prompt account mislabels them — potentially undermining the theory's explanation of its own case, not just of other settings.

The 'conserved total maintenance effort' backbone is inferred from the observed unchanged logged hours and meeting time rather than independently predicted, and its zero-sum implication (within-unit must RISE to absorb freed effort) is only half-supported by the phenomenon card ('stayed the same or increased'). The theory offers no criterion for when a flat within-unit result would falsify conservation.

The claim that existing constructs 'cannot generate a pattern in which total logged hours and meeting time are unchanged while only the boundary-crossing subset collapses' overreaches: Zuzul et al. (2025, Management Science) and Suh et al. (2011, JMIS) already establish the composition outcome and document the boundary-selective pattern. The 'why existing insufficient' argument omits the most directly relevant composition-based literature.

No measurement rule is given to classify a tie as 'ambient-prompted discretionary' versus 'role-mandated' independent of whether it survived, so the mechanism is not operationalizable against the ties (cross-unit but mandated) that are most diagnostic.

The assumption field honestly states that cross-boundary maintenance 'depended on an ambient prompt rather than on the tie's recognized value', but this is asserted as a premise, not tested against the alternative that cross-boundary ties lapsed because their recognized value was genuinely lower — an alternative the theory does not rule out.

[HARD LANGUAGE REQUIREMENT] For this task, all final structured-output field content (not just your thinking) must be written in English — do not switch to any other language for the substantive content, even if it would otherwise feel natural to you. Established theory names, author citations, and technical terms may keep their standard form. This requirement takes priority over any default habit implied elsewhere in the task instructions.

---

You are a top-journal reviewer known for rigor, specializing in taking apart theoretical claims that sound
fluent but aren't actually sound. You are now deployed as the execution agent for Step 5 of ATBA (Abductive
Theory-Building Agent): "Adversarial Interrogation" — **the sole reason this step exists is to create
genuine adversarial pressure**: you have no idea how the candidate theory below was constructed, what
scoring or filtering it went through, or which part its author thinks is strongest — you are given only
the theory's own content. Do not presume it "should be sound"; your default posture is skepticism, not
helping it sound more convincing.

## Input

You will receive (**and only receive**):
- **The phenomenon card** (Step 1's output) and **the research question** (Step 3's output): as objective
  background for judging whether this theoretical explanation genuinely answers the question and whether
  its boundary conditions are reasonable — not the candidate's own author's self-defense.
- **The candidate theory itself**: `candidate_name`, `theory_elements` (X/Y/relation form/mechanism/
  assumption/boundary conditions), its mechanism-borrowing pattern (within-tradition deepening /
  adjacent-tradition bridging / cross-tradition borrowing), which existing construct it borrows/modifies,
  why the existing construct falls short, and its full explanatory argument for the phenomenon —
  **if the borrowing pattern is cross-tradition borrowing, you'll also get the candidate author's own
  `disanalogy_note`** (where this mechanism doesn't transfer cleanly). This self-disclosure is itself a
  prime target for interrogation: did the author honestly disclose the truly serious mismatch, or did they
  dress up a fatal disanalogy as a minor caveat?

You will **not** receive: this candidate's four-virtue scores, novelty-check verdict, Lakatos judgment, or
why it was selected over the others — all of that is the generating side's own meta-reasoning; you must
judge independently, may not cite content you were never given, and may not assume the generating side
already checked some issue so you can skip it.

## Task: three question types, each answered honestly

For the given candidate theory, pose and answer at least one of each of the following three question types
(add more if the theory's specifics warrant it):

1. **Falsifiability**: what observation would refute this theory? If the candidate's phrasing is vague
   enough that "whatever is observed can be explained away," that's a serious signal and should be judged
   `fails`.
2. **Boundary conditions**: does this mechanism still hold in a different setting (different industry,
   culture, organization size...)? Does the candidate's `assumption` field honestly state the premise it
   depends on, or does it dodge the conditions under which the mechanism would break down?
3. **Relabeling suspicion**: is this just an existing construct with a new name attached? You have
   `search_scopus`/`get_paper_abstract` tools (usage in the "Retrieval Skill" section below) — **do not
   simply take the candidate's own claim of "borrows/modifies construct X" at face value**; independently
   search to verify whether this core mechanism already has an equivalent formulation in the literature. If
   your search turns up a highly similar existing construct — even one the candidate never mentioned —
   report it honestly. Put whatever you found in this independent search into that
   `InterrogationRecord.cited_evidence` (title + authors + year + the snippet supporting your judgment +
   the original abstract) — don't just paraphrase it in `assessment`; reviewers need to be able to check
   your basis.

**If the mechanism-borrowing pattern is `cross_tradition_borrowing`, add a fourth question type**: does
the candidate's self-disclosed `disanalogy_note` actually hold up? Is the real mismatch in the borrowed
mechanism more serious than the candidate itself admits — e.g., it admits "some detail needs adjusting,"
but you judge that this "detail" is actually the load-bearing premise the borrowed mechanism depends on,
and adjusting it hollows the mechanism out entirely. This kind of "dressing up a fatal disanalogy as a
minor caveat" should be judged `fails`, not `weak`.

For each question type:
- `question` must be specific to this theory's actual content (name its X/Y/mechanism) — not a generic
  template like "is this theory falsifiable?"
- `assessment` may only be judged from the given candidate content (plus whatever you retrieve yourself) —
  you may not make assumptions favorable to the candidate by invoking a creation process you were never
  told about.
- `verdict`: `withstands` (current phrasing already answers this well) / `weak` (answers it but the
  argument is thin — worth strengthening, not a core-mechanism flaw) / `fails` (cannot be reasonably
  answered, and points to the core mechanism itself not holding up).

## Honestly flag weaknesses

Even when the overall verdict is `withstands`, list any question that didn't fully convince you in
`unanswered_weaknesses` — **the interrogation record is also something you wrote, but that doesn't mean
you can hide findings unfavorable to the candidate**; hiding weaknesses would defeat the entire point of
ATBA's "auditable" selling point.

## Overall verdict and loop-back

- Any question `verdict=fails` → `overall_verdict=fails`, and you must:
  1. Give a concrete revision instruction in `loop_back_instruction`: name which question, which part
     doesn't hold up, and what needs to change — not just "come up with something better."
  2. **Fill in `loop_back_target_field`** (new this round, required): pin the revision instruction above
     to one specific field of the candidate theory — e.g., if the mechanism itself doesn't hold up, fill
     `mechanism`; if the borrowed construct is simply the wrong fit, fill `borrowed_or_modified_construct`;
     if the explanatory argument for the phenomenon has a hole, fill `explanation_of_phenomenon`. **Only
     fill `whole_candidate` when the core mechanism as a whole doesn't hold up and genuinely cannot be
     pinned to one specific field** — don't default to it out of convenience. Step 4's revision will use
     this field to decide between "rewrite only this one field" and "reconstruct the whole candidate";
     the more precise the location, the less the revision will disturb parts of the candidate that were
     never actually a problem.
- No `fails` but some `weak` → `overall_verdict=weak`, `loop_back_instruction` left empty (no loop-back
  triggered — the weakness is recorded and the pipeline proceeds normally).
- All `withstands` → `overall_verdict=withstands`.

Call the tool `report_step5_output` to give the final result. Do not output any text outside the tool
call.

## Retrieval Skill: How to Use the `search_scopus` and `get_paper_abstract` Tools Well

You have two tools:
- `search_scopus(query, max_results)` — give it a Scopus concept query and it automatically adds the
  UTD24 journal-range restriction and returns real results (a paper list + total hit count). **You must
  decide for yourself what to search, how many rounds to run, and when you have searched enough** — a
  single tool call is not enough. This is the most important part of this skill: search is a process you
  drive by judging results and adjusting, not "generate one query and stop."
- `get_paper_abstract(doi)` — the paper list `search_scopus` returns does not itself carry
  abstracts (a Scopus API limitation); to read a paper's full abstract, look it up by its `doi` (not
  `scopus_id`) with this tool, which internally tries Semantic Scholar then OpenAlex. **Only call it for papers you have decided to cite** (i.e. ones going into the final
  `cited_evidence`) — most search results only serve to judge "is this query on target," and the papers
  you actually end up citing are usually just a few; fetching an abstract for every hit wastes quota.
  Conversely, **before deciding to cite a paper, you must fetch its abstract first** — don't judge
  whether a paper supports/contradicts a conclusion from the title alone; a title rarely reveals which
  specific mechanism the paper actually covers.

### Scopus query syntax

- `TITLE-ABS-KEY()`: searches title, abstract, and keywords together (most common, broadest coverage —
  default to this)
- `TITLE()` / `ABS()` / `KEY()`: title / abstract / keywords only
- `AUTH()`: author name; `PUBYEAR`: publication year; `DOCTYPE()`: document type (ar=article, re=review)
- Boolean operators `AND`/`OR`/`AND NOT`, parentheses for grouping, quotes for phrases, `*` for wildcards
- Write only the concept part — **do not construct the journal-range restriction yourself** (the
  EXACTSRCTITLE-based UTD24 filter is added automatically by the tool)
- If what you're searching for is originally in Chinese, translate it into standard English academic
  terminology in your own understanding first, then build the query — Scopus indexes mostly
  English-language literature

### Don't stack too many ANDs — recall first, narrow later

A real case we actually hit (run `4b637242b0d24fa097444362d23ffb66`): 6 consecutive searches on the
same direction, and the first 5 came back at zero or near-zero hits, all for the same reason — the
query ANDed 3-4 independent concept clusters together, e.g.:

- `entrepreneur* AND narrative* AND investor* AND (decept* OR fraud OR ...)` — 0 hits
- `entrepreneur* AND (fraud OR deception) AND (narrative OR storytelling OR story OR account)` — 0 hits

Once `AND` was cut down to just 1-2 concept clusters, the same underlying concepts started hitting
right away:
- `"entrepreneurial storytelling" OR "entrepreneurial narrative" OR "cultural entrepreneurship"` —
  26 hits
- `entrepreneur* AND storytell* AND (fraud OR deception OR fabricat* OR "false narrative")` — 1 hit

**Why**: `TITLE-ABS-KEY()` only searches a small span of text — title, abstract, and keywords. The
odds that a single paper's abstract literally mentions 3-4 independent concept clusters at once
(even with synonyms ORed within each cluster) are inherently low — most papers foreground only one or
two of your concepts. More `AND`s means exponentially fewer hits; this is a query **structure**
problem, not evidence the literature doesn't exist.

**What to actually do**:
- **Keep the number of independent `AND`-joined concept clusters per query to at most 2, rarely 3**
  (not counting the journal filter, which the tool adds automatically) — beyond 3 `AND`-joined
  clusters, you'll very likely get zero hits no matter how you tweak the synonyms.
- **When a level "misses," your first instinct should be to drop one `AND` cluster (loosen the
  structure), not keep the same `AND` structure and just swap synonyms** — rewording fixes "bad
  phrasing this one time"; cutting an `AND` fixes "the structure was too picky to begin with." These
  are different problems. Several rewrite-retries that keep the same number of `AND` clusters and only
  change wording will likely all fail the same way (exactly what happened in the case above: 4
  consecutive rewrites kept the same AND structure before someone finally thought to loosen it).
- When you want to express several concepts at once, prefer **ORing synonyms within the same `AND`
  cluster** to raise the hit rate for one concept, rather than adding a new `AND` cluster to "pin it
  down precisely" — the latter is a precision mindset; this step needs recall. Judging exactly which
  part of the mechanism a paper covers is your job after you've read it, not something the query
  string should be filtering for.

### Three-level degrading search protocol (core strategy — follow it strictly)

For each mechanism/proposition you need to check, try the following levels in order — **every hit must
be labeled with which level it was found at**; a hit at "the broad disciplinary level" is explicitly
less credible than a hit at "the exact-mechanism level," and the two must never be conflated:

1. **Exact-mechanism match**: phrase the query as close as possible to the specific mechanism wording
   (e.g. something specific enough to map directly onto one particular part).
2. **If it misses, or hits are too few/clearly irrelevant, drop to the theory-family level**: switch to
   the broader theoretical tradition/construct family this direction belongs to.
3. **If the theory-family level still misses, drop to the broad disciplinary level**: the whole
   direction's broad literature, no longer requiring an exact match to the specific mechanism.

**Rewrite-and-retry rule**: keyword/semantic search is sensitive to wording — **before declaring any
level a "miss," you must first rephrase the query and search once more**, to rule out "a false negative
purely from bad phrasing this one time" — you may not drop to the next level just because the first
attempt at a level came back empty. **A rewrite is not just swapping synonyms** — if the previous query
ANDed 3+ concept clusters, your first choice for the rewrite should be dropping one `AND` cluster
(loosen the structure, see above), not keeping the same `AND` structure and changing a few words; only
reach for synonym swaps once the `AND` structure is already lean (1-2 clusters). In other words, each of
the three levels may take up to two searches (original phrasing + one rewrite).

**When all levels and their rewrites are exhausted with no hit**: report honestly that this is "not
covered by retrieval" — **this is not a failure**, it is a legitimate conclusion; attach every query you
actually tried and its hit count as evidence that you genuinely searched and came up empty.

**If a hit already fully explains what you're checking**: report that honestly — do not keep searching
to "prove there's something here," and do not selectively ignore that literature.

### After each search, ask yourself

- Does this result's volume and relevance mean I should keep dropping levels, or can I stop here?
- If results are zero or few: is it a wording problem (rewrite and retry) or does this level genuinely
  have nothing (drop a level)?
- If results are plentiful but none quite on point: is the query too broad (tighten it), or does this
  direction genuinely have a lot of literature that never touches the specific point you're checking
  (which is itself a "hit but the mechanism isn't covered" signal)?

**Audit requirement**: when you finish, you must be able to state **every** query you actually used with
`search_scopus` (including rewrite-retry versions) — not just the last successful one; the complete trail
is an audit requirement, not optional.

## Phenomenon card (objective background, not the candidate theory author's self-justification)
actor: A large technology company and its workforce — employees, organized into different functional groups, who communicate with one another in the course of their jobs.
observed_behavior: After the entire workforce moved from working in shared offices to working full-time from separate locations, employees' work-related contacts stayed mostly within their own functional group and changed little from one period to the next, instead of reaching across different functional groups.
field_constraints: The whole workforce of one large technology company; the change was a shift to full-time remote work; internal records of employees' communication were collected both before and after the shift; total logged working hours and total meeting time were almost the same in the two periods.
apparent_motive: (none)
observable_outcome: The number of contacts that linked employees in different functional groups fell sharply after the shift, while contacts among employees within the same functional group stayed the same or increased; the totals of logged working hours and meeting time were roughly unchanged between the two periods.

## Research question (objective background)
Why does removing physical co-location from an entire organization's workforce — while total logged working hours and meeting time are preserved — selectively collapse ties that cross functional boundaries while leaving ties within functional units intact or strengthened? ## Candidate theory under interrogation: Conserved Interaction Budget: Discretionary Ties Decay as Effort Reallocates to Role-Anchored Ties

content.abstract: Workplace communications around the world were drastically altered by the COVID-19 pandemic, related work-from-home orders, and the rise of remote work. To understand these shifts, we analyzed aggregated, anonymized metadata from over 360 billion emails within 4,361 organizations worldwide. By comparing month-to-month and year-over-year metrics, we examined changes in network community structures over the 24 months before and after COVID-19. We also examined shifts across multiple communication media (email, instant message, video call, and calendaring software) within a single global organization and compared them with communications shifts that were driven by changes in formal organizational structure. We found that in 2020, organizations around the world became more siloed than in 2019, evidenced by increased modularity. This shift was concurrent with decreased stability within silos. Collectively, our analyses indicate that following the onset of COVID-19, employees’ communications began to shift more dynamically between subcommunities (teams, workgroups, or functional areas). At the same time, once in a subcommunity, they limited their communication to other members of that community. We term these network changes dynamic silos. We provide initial insights into the meaning and implications of dynamic silos for the future of work. This paper was accepted by Lamar Pierce, organizations. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2022.02797 .

We examine how the virtuality of work context influences individuals' social networks within and across work groups. Given this purpose, we develop a multilevel research framework that explores the effects of different levels of virtuality on one's intra-group tie strength and extra-group network range based on the computer-mediated communication theory, the proximity theory, and the social network theory. The results of the hierarchical linear modeling indicate that the individual-level virtuality (use of personal and communal communication technologies) significantly influences one's intra-group tie strength and extra-group network range. Moreover, the results show that the effects of individual-level virtuality on social networks vary depending on the group-level virtuality, such as geographic/temporal dispersion and technological support. By illuminating how individuals' social networks can be developed through the appropriate use of personal and communal communication technologies in the context of a virtual group, this study provides useful insights into the mechanics that underlie effective virtual work.

Reducing the physical distance among R&D engineers and between R&D and marketing is widely believed to result in more frequent communication, and hence higher product development performance. However, the empirical evidence for the effect of co-location on communication frequency is problematic for two reasons: (1) the evidence often features either little contextual realism or doubtful internal validity, and (2) the analysis does not deal with the statistical problems typical of network data. Our study avoids the first problem by using sequential network data collected from a quasi-experiment at an industrial company that regrouped its R&D teams into a new facility. We avoid the second problem by using Wasserman and Iacobucci's (1988) method for the statistical analysis of sequential network data. Our results show that communication among R&D teams was enhanced after co-locating these teams. Surprisingly, communication frequency between R&D and marketing was not affected by the increased physical distance. This may suggest that business procedures accompanying the relocation prevented a widening gap between R&D and marketing. Alternatively, it may indicate that the effect of co-location depends on the content and medium of the communication flows.

Whereas most research on network evolution has focused on the role of interaction opportunities in the formation of new ties, this paper addresses tie decay choices. When the opportunity structure gets reorganized, social actors make choices about which ties to retain and which to allow to decay, informed by their past experience of the tie. I argue that, conditional on changes in opportunity, people (especially those with Machiavellian personalities) choose to retain ties to valuable contacts, they retain reciprocated ties (especially with highly empathic others), and they retain socially embedded ties (especially if they are low self-monitors). The empirical design, which exploits a randomized natural experiment, confirms these hypotheses and suggests that our understanding of tie decay choices—and, consequently, of network evolution—is enhanced by an integrated theoretical perspective that encompasses both social structure and social psychology. This paper was accepted by Olav Sorenson, organizations.

Models of network formation emphasize the importance of social similarity and propinquity in producing strong interpersonal connections. The positive effect each factor can have on tie strength has been documented across a number of studies, and yet we know surprisingly very little about how the two factors combine to produce strong ties. Being in close proximity could either amplify or dampen the positive effect that social similarity can have on tie strength. Data on tie strength among teachers working in five public schools were analyzed to shed light on this theoretical question. The empirical results indicate that teachers who were similar in age were more likely to be connected by a strong tie, especially teachers for whom age similarity was more likely to be salient. Moreover, teachers who took breaks at the same time or who had classrooms on the same floor communicated more frequently and felt more emotionally attached. Among the public school teachers, propinquity amplified the positive effect that age similarity had on tie strength. The strongest network connections occurred among age-similar teachers who had classrooms on the same floor. The empirical results illustrate the value of considering how social similarity and propinquity contribute to strong ties independently and when combined with each other.

The Coronavirus disease (COVID-19) pandemic has prompted an unprecedented shift to remote work. Workers across the globe have used digital technologies to connect with teammates and others in their organizations. In what ways did the COVID-19 crisis alter the frequency and balance of internal and external team interactions? During a crisis, networking offers a type of goal-directed behavior through which individuals source and provide information. We can understand how people use their network through the lens of network churn, changes in embeddedness brought on by the creation, dissolution, and/or reactivation of network ties. higher We posit that performing individuals exhibit distinct networking strategies as compared to lower performing employees during the pandemic. We present a field study conducted in a multinational industrial manufacturing company in China investigating network churn during the COVID-19 pandemic. Findings show that, during a crisis, job performance is positively related to the volume of inter-team tie creation and inter-team tie reactivation, but not intra-team tie creation and intra-team tie reactivation. Job performance is not related to the volume of intra- and inter-team tie dissolution. The study provides early, yet important insights into the interplay between crisis and organizational social networks. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2021 APA, all rights reserved).

content.abstract: Using a longitudinal dataset of research collaborations over 15 years at Stanford University, we build a theory of intraorganizational task relationships that distinguishes the different factors associated with the formation and persistence of network ties. We highlight six factors: shared organizational foci, shared traits and interests, tie advantages from popularity, tie reinforcement from third parties, tie strength and multiplexity, and the instrumental returns from the products of ties. Findings suggest that ties form when unfamiliar people identify desirable and matching traits in potential partners. By contrast, ties persist when familiar people reflect on the quality of their relationship and shared experiences. The former calls for shallow, short-term strategies for assessing a broad array of potential ties; the latter calls for long-term strategies and substantive assessments of a relationship’s worth so as to draw extended rewards from the association. This suggests that organizational activities geared toward sustaining persistent intraorganizational task relationships need to be different from activities aimed at forging new ones.

This study takes an affiliative coping theory perspective to examine whether working adults reactivated dormant ties with individuals they had not contacted for at least 3 years to cope with stressors experienced due to the COVID-19 pandemic. Stressors originating in the workplace (job insecurity and remote work) and in the family (stressful familial social ties) were examined in a sample of 232 working adults in the southeastern United States. Individuals were more likely to reactivate their dormant ties when their job was insecure, and the magnitude of the reactivations was greater among individuals experiencing stressful social ties with family members than those not experiencing those stressors. We also found that there was a significant interaction between remote work and having a stressful tie within the household in dormant tie reactivation. Although previous theory has focused mostly on the benefits of frequent, active social relationships for coping, our results suggest that reactivating dormant ties might be a coping mechanism as well. Our study also suggests that workplace dormant tie research should broaden its focus beyond exchanged instrumental support to consider emotional support that might be transferred during reactivation. In particular, is the Y — the allocation of work-related contact across boundary-crossing vs boundary-contained ties as a function of co-location/virtuality — already an established dependent variable, and is the observed pattern (within-group ties hold/rise while cross-group ties collapse) already documented, such that the candidate's claim that 'existing constructs cannot generate a pattern in which total logged hours and meeting time are unchanged while only the boundary-crossing subset collapses' overreaches?
input.assessment: I searched independently rather than trusting the candidate's self-report that it merely 'modifies Kleinbaum (2018)'. Two findings cut against the novelty claim for the Y and the phenomenon: (1) Suh, Shin, Ahuja & Kim (2011, JMIS) explicitly model 'intra-group tie strength and extra-group network range' as the dependent variable of virtuality — the composition outcome is already an established construct; (2) Zuzul et al. (2025, Management Science), analyzing 360B+ emails across 4,361 organizations through the COVID co-location shock, document exactly the boundary-selective pattern the candidate claims anchor theory 'cannot generate': organizations 'became more siloed... evidenced by increased modularity' and employees 'limited their communication to other members of that community'. That is the phenomenon, in the anchor journal, uncited. So the claim that existing constructs cannot generate a composition-only shift is contradicted empirically. cited_evidence.title: Dynamic Silos: Increased Modularity and Decreased Stability in Intraorganizational Communication Networks During the COVID-19 Pandemic
cited_evidence.relevant_snippet: We found that in 2020, organizations around the world became more siloed than in 2019, evidenced by increased modularity. This shift was concurrent with decreased stability within silos. ... At the same time, once in a subcommunity, they limited their communication to other members of that community. We term these network changes dynamic silos.
cited_evidence.abstract: Workplace communications around the world were drastically altered by the COVID-19 pandemic, related work-from-home orders, and the rise of remote work. To understand these shifts, we analyzed aggregated, anonymized metadata from over 360 billion emails within 4,361 organizations worldwide. By comparing month-to-month and year-over-year metrics, we examined changes in network community structures over the 24 months before and after COVID-19. We also examined shifts across multiple communication media (email, instant message, video call, and calendaring software) within a single global organization and compared them with communications shifts that were driven by changes in formal organizational structure. We found that in 2020, organizations around the world became more siloed than in 2019, evidenced by increased modularity. This shift was concurrent with decreased stability within silos. Collectively, our analyses indicate that following the onset of COVID-19, employees' communications began to shift more dynamically between subcommunities (teams, workgroups, or functional areas). At the same time, once in a subcommunity, they limited their communication to other members of that community. We term these network changes dynamic silos. We provide initial insights into the meaning and implications of dynamic silos for the future of work. This paper was accepted by Lamar Pierce, organizations.

Given this purpose, we develop a multilevel research framework that explores the effects of different levels of virtuality on one's intra-group tie strength and extra-group network range based on the computer-mediated communication theory, the proximity theory, and the social network theory. The results of the hierarchical linear modeling indicate that the individual-level virtuality (use of personal and communal communication technologies) significantly influences one's intra-group tie strength and extra-group network range. Moreover, the results show that the effects of individual-level virtuality on social networks vary depending on the group-level virtuality, such as geographic/temporal dispersion and technological support. By illuminating how individuals' social networks can be developed through the appropriate use of personal and communal communication technologies in the context of a virtual group, this study provides useful insights into the mechanics that underlie effective virtual work.

cited_evidence.abstract: Whereas most research on network evolution has focused on the role of interaction opportunities in the formation of new ties, this paper addresses tie decay choices. When the opportunity structure gets reorganized, social actors make choices about which ties to retain and which to allow to decay, informed by their past experience of the tie. I argue that, conditional on changes in opportunity, people (especially those with Machiavellian personalities) choose to retain ties to valuable contacts, they retain reciprocated ties (especially with highly empathic others), and they retain socially embedded ties (especially if they are low self-monitors). The empirical design, which exploits a randomized natural experiment, confirms these hypotheses and suggests that our understanding of tie decay choices—and, consequently, of network evolution—is enhanced by an integrated theoretical perspective that encompasses both social structure and social psychology. This paper was accepted by Olav Sorenson, organizations.

cited_evidence.relevant_snippet: Our results show that communication among R&D teams was enhanced after co-locating these teams. Surprisingly, communication frequency between R&D and marketing was not affected by the increased physical distance. This may suggest that business procedures accompanying the relocation prevented a widening gap between R&D and marketing. Alternatively, it may indicate that the effect of co-location depends on the content and medium of the communication flows.
cited_evidence.abstract: Reducing the physical distance among R&D engineers and between R&D and marketing is widely believed to result in more frequent communication, and hence higher product development performance. However, the empirical evidence for the effect of co-location on communication frequency is problematic for two reasons: (1) the evidence often features either little contextual realism or doubtful internal validity, and (2) the analysis does not deal with the statistical problems typical of network data. Our study avoids the first problem by using sequential network data collected from a quasi-experiment at an industrial company that regrouped its R&D teams into a new facility. We avoid the second problem by using Wasserman and Iacobucci's (1988) method for the statistical analysis of sequential network data. Our results show that communication among R&D teams was enhanced after co-locating these teams. Surprisingly, communication frequency between R&D and marketing was not affected by the increased physical distance. This may suggest that business procedures accompanying the relocation prevented a widening gap between R&D and marketing. Alternatively, it may indicate that the effect of co-location depends on the content and medium of the communication flows.
